lead: Classical physics draws a particle as a point with a sharp position and a sharp momentum at every instant. Quantum mechanics does not allow both to be sharp at the same time. The product of the spread in position, Δx, and the spread in momentum, Δp, has a smallest possible value, ℏ/2. The same limit links energy spread ΔE and time spread Δt. This uncertainty is not a bad measurement; it is a property of matter waves. It fixes natural spectral linewidths, the least kinetic energy of a trapped particle, and the limits of imaging an electron.
prereq: You need: matter waves, wave packets and group velocity, and single-slit diffraction from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call this Heisenberg's uncertainty principle. For a particle described by a matter wave, let Δx be the spread in position about its mean and Δp the spread in momentum about its mean. The bound is:

blocks.where: Δx is the root-mean-square spread in position; Δp is the root-mean-square spread in momentum; ℏ = h/(2π) = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s is the reduced Planck constant.

blocks.text: ℏ is the reduced Planck constant and h is Planck's constant. A state with a very small Δx must have a large Δp, and the reverse. The bound uses this precise spread about the mean. Estimates treat Δx and Δp as typical ranges, so only the order of magnitude matters.

blocks.where: ΔE is the spread in energy; Δt is the lifetime of the state or the time available for a measurement.

blocks.text: A state with exactly known energy has ΔE = 0, so Δt is infinite: it lasts forever. For classical waves the same idea appears as Δx Δk ≥ 1/2, where Δk is the spread in wave number. For matter waves p = ℏk, so Δp = ℏ Δk, and the classical wave relation becomes Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2.

sections.h3: Why a narrow slit broadens the pattern

blocks.text: Send an electron wave through a slit of width a. The slit limits where the electron can be, so Δx is of order a. After the slit, the wave diffracts. Unit 2 gives the first minimum of a single slit at a sin θ = λ, where λ is the de Broglie wavelength and θ is the angle from the centre.

Before the slit the momentum is along the beam, p = h/λ. After the slit the transverse momentum can be as large as p sin θ. Using the first minimum, p sin θ ≈ (h/λ)(λ/a) = h/a. Thus Δp is of order h/a. The product is Δx Δp ≈ a(h/a) = h, which is of the order of ℏ and obeys the bound.

Narrow slit: small Δx, broad diffraction, large Δp. Wide slit: large Δx, narrow diffraction, small Δp. The slit does not push the electron; the wave simply has no sharp transverse momentum until a measurement is made.

A classical trajectory needs a sharp x(t) and a sharp p(t) at each instant, so that the points join into a line. If Δx and Δp cannot both be small, no such sharp line exists. The electron has a cloud of possible positions and momenta, not a railway track.

items: Natural linewidth. An excited atom lives for a time τ. Treat τ as Δt. Then ΔE ≥ ℏ/(2τ), and the frequency width is Δν = ΔE/h ≈ 1/(4πτ). A lifetime of 10 ns gives Δν ≈ 8 MHz. This is the natural linewidth of the spectral line.

Zero-point energy. A particle trapped in a region of size L has Δx ≈ L, so Δp ≳ ℏ/(2L). Its kinetic energy cannot be zero: K ≈ (Δp)²/(2m) is of order ℏ²/(2mL²). In a harmonic trap the exact least energy is ½ℏω, where ω is the trap angular frequency. The particle keeps moving even at absolute zero.

Gamma-ray microscope, qualitatively. To locate an electron, a photon is scattered from it. A shorter photon wavelength λ gives a smaller Δx, but the photon carries momentum h/λ and gives a larger unknown kick to the electron, so Δp is larger. A longer wavelength gives a smaller kick but a blurred position. The product cannot fall below ℏ/2.

figure.caption: An electron wave passes a narrow slit and spreads by diffraction. The narrow slit makes Δx small, so the spread in transverse momentum Δp becomes large and the product stays at or above ℏ/2.

spec.title: Uncertainty from a slit
spec.aria: An electron wave passes a narrow slit, spreads by diffraction, and sets the uncertainty product at least h-bar over two.

examples.question: An electron is confined to a region of size Δx = 0.1 nm. Estimate the minimum momentum uncertainty and the kinetic energy from Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2. Use ℏ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s and m = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg.
steps: Convert the size: Δx = 0.1 nm = 0.1 × 10⁻⁹ m = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁰ m.
Convert to electronvolt using 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J: K = 1.527 × 10⁻¹⁹ / 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ = 0.953 eV, about 0.95 eV.
examples.answer: The minimum momentum uncertainty is about 5.28 × 10⁻²⁵ kg·m/s, and the corresponding kinetic energy is about 1.53 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, or 0.95 eV.

dx = 0.1e-9

dp = hbar / (2 * dx)
K = dp**2 / (2 * m)

traps: Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2 is a lower bound, not an equality. Do not set Δx Δp = ℏ/2 unless the question asks for the minimum.
Use ℏ = h/(2π), not h. Mixing h and ℏ changes the answer by a factor 2π.
A particle in a trap can have average momentum zero while Δp is not zero. The spread enters the bound, not the average.
Δx is a spread about the mean, not the full width of a slit or box. The slit width or box length only sets the order of magnitude.
The energy-time relation does not mean energy disappears for a short time. It says a short-lived state has a spread in energy.

quiz.q: State the position-momentum uncertainty relation and define each symbol.
quiz.a: Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2, where Δx is the spread in position, Δp is the spread in momentum, and ℏ is the reduced Planck constant, h/(2π).

quiz.q: Why does a narrower slit produce a wider diffraction pattern for an electron wave?
quiz.a: A narrower slit makes Δx smaller. The matter wave then has a larger spread in transverse wave number, so Δp is larger, and the diffraction angle increases. The product still obeys Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2.

quiz.q: An electron is confined to Δx = 0.20 nm. Estimate the minimum Δp using ℏ = 1.055 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s.
An excited state has lifetime 2.0 ns. Estimate its natural linewidth in Hz.
Write the classical wave uncertainty relation linking Δx and Δk.
quiz.a: Δx Δk ≥ 1/2. For matter waves p = ℏk, so Δp = ℏΔk and this gives Δx Δp ≥ ℏ/2.

quiz.q: Does ΔE Δt ≥ ℏ/2 allow violation of energy conservation? Explain.
quiz.a: No. It says a state that lasts only a short time Δt has a spread ΔE in its energy. A very short-lived state is not a state of exactly sharp energy. Energy conservation still holds for the full process; the spread is a property of the state, not free energy.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same bound sets the standard quantum limit of interferometers used to detect tiny displacements, and squeezed light is one way to push below it. Atomic clocks use long-lived transitions, so their linewidth is small but never zero. In nanoscale devices, zero-point motion limits how cold a mechanical oscillator can be. Search next: standard quantum limit, squeezed states, natural linewidth, zero-point energy.
